summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option that a Dual-Stack Lite B4 element uses to discover the IPv6 address of its corresponding AFTR, the Address Family Transition Router.

eli5.summary: A home router needs to know where the provider's translating machine is. This gives the provider a way to tell it, using the normal automatic configuration messages.

questions: what is the dhcpv6 aftr name option
how does a b4 find its aftr
subtitle: A single DHCPv6 option that tells a Dual-Stack Lite home gateway where its carrier-side tunnel endpoint is.

tldr.problem: A Dual-Stack Lite B4 device does not know whether its network offers the service, and if it did, it would not know the remote end of the IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnel (the softwire).
tldr.mechanism: The AFTR-Name DHCPv6 option (code 64) carries the fully qualified domain name of the AFTR. The B4 asks for it in its Option Request option, then resolves the name to an IPv6 address with a AAAA lookup.
tldr.outcome: A configured AFTR name both locates the tunnel endpoint and signals that the B4 should start DS-Lite service. Proposed Standard, with no later RFC listed as replacing it.

today: RFC 6334 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2011, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with Dual-Stack Lite as defined in RFC 6333.

sections.title: Why the B4 Needs an AFTR Name
sections.content:
Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333) offers both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity to customers who are given only an IPv6 prefix, with no IPv4 address on the attachment device. A key part of it is an IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnel, called a softwire.

A DS-Lite Basic Bridging BroadBand (B4) device has two gaps. It does not know whether its network offers DS-Lite, and it does not know the remote endpoint of the tunnel. This RFC closes both with one DHCPv6 option that carries the Address Family Transition Router (AFTR) location as a DNS hostname. Once the B4 has that configuration, it also knows to start DS-Lite service and become a softwire initiator.

How the B4 then builds the IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire is out of scope for this document.
sections.eli5: Your router has a message to deliver across a special tunnel, but nobody told it where the tunnel starts. This RFC is how the provider hands over that address.

sections.title: The AFTR-Name Option Format
sections.content:
The option has the usual DHCPv6 option-code and option-len fields, plus a variable-length tunnel-endpoint-name holding a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the AFTR the client MAY connect to. The option code is OPTION_AFTR_NAME, value 64. It SHOULD NOT appear in any DHCPv6 messages other than Solicit, Advertise, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reply.

The name is encoded as DHCPv6 requires for domain names: one octet giving the length of a DNS label (at most 63 octets), then the label itself, repeated for every label, ending with a zero-length label. The RFC's example is aftr.example.com., which has a tunnel-endpoint-name length of 18 octets, so option-len is 18.

A client validates the option and requires all of these to hold:

  • option-len is greater than 3;
  • option-len is no more than the octets remaining in the DHCPv6 packet;
  • the individual label lengths do not exceed the option length;
  • the name has a valid DHCPv6 domain-name format;
  • there are no compression tags;
  • there is at least one label of nonzero length.
sections.eli5: The option is a small label with a code number, a length, and the machine's name spelled out one word at a time, each word starting with how long it is.

sections.title: What the DHCPv6 Server Does
sections.content:
A server SHOULD NOT send more than one AFTR-Name option, and SHOULD NOT allow several names to be configured inside one option. Clients treat both cases as exceptions, so an operator whose server software does not check this must be careful not to configure multiple domain names.

The option follows the normal request rules of DHCPv6. A server will not reply with an AFTR-Name option unless the client listed it in its Option Request option (OPTION_ORO).
sections.eli5: The provider's server only gives out one name, and only if the router asked for it, like a shop that hands over a leaflet only when you ask.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
A client that supports the B4 role and follows this RFC MUST include OPTION_AFTR_NAME in its OPTION_ORO. Because it needs DNS to turn the name into an address, it MAY also ask for OPTION_DNS_SERVERS (RFC 3646). The RFC calls the combination of DHCPv6 client and B4 element the B4 system, since in practice they may be integrated or separate.

On receiving the option, the B4 system MUST verify it. If there is more than one AFTR-Name option, it MUST use only the first. If one option holds several FQDNs (shown by several root labels), it MUST use only the first FQDN.

It then does a standard DNS lookup for a AAAA record (RFC 3596). If the answer holds more than one IPv6 address, it picks one as the remote tunnel endpoint. It MUST NOT establish more than one DS-Lite tunnel at the same time per interface.

A device with several interfaces handles each separately. If several networks supply the option, the B4 system MUST configure a tunnel for each interface, because each tunnel provides IPv4 connectivity for one interface. How an AFTR-Name is bound to an interface is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The router asks for the name, looks it up like a phone book to find the real address, and picks one address if there are several. It builds one tunnel per network connection, not more.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it presents no new security issues. It warns that, as with all DHCPv6-derived configuration, the setting may come from a third party in the middle. There is therefore no basis for trusting the access level of the DS-Lite softwire connection, and DS-Lite should not bypass security mechanisms such as IP firewalls.

For wider coverage it points to RFC 3315 for DHCPv6 security issues and RFC 6333 for DS-Lite security issues.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky could pretend to be the provider and give your router a wrong name, so the tunnel should not get any special trust.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has allocated a single DHCPv6 option code, 64, referencing this document, for OPTION_AFTR_NAME. The RFC creates no other registry entries.
sections.eli5: The official list of option numbers now has number 64 reserved for this option.
